title: Killing innocents
hook: the Qur'an: whoever kills a soul unjustly, it's as if he killed all humanity (5:32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, rejecting extremism, and a letter that answered a self-declared caliph point by point. Your line was scholars said no. Did you read a statement through? Today, the verse underneath that no. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

Two brothers, the sons of Adam, each bring an offering. One is accepted, one isn't. The one who was refused says, I will kill you. And the other answers, in the Qur'an's telling, that even if his brother reaches out a hand to kill him, he won't reach out his own to kill. Then it happens anyway. Afterward the killer doesn't even know what to do with the body, until a raven scratches at the ground and shows him. That's Surah al-Ma'idah. And straight after the grave comes the verse.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, TWO OFFERINGS.` → `I WON'T RAISE MY HAND.` → `A RAVEN AND A GRAVE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in Pickthall: "whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind." Three things in that sentence. First, who. The Arabic word is nafs, a soul, a living person. Not a believer, not a neighbor, not one of us. A human being. Second, the arithmetic. One death counts as all of humanity. The verse refuses to let a single killing be small, or to let anyone say it was only one. And it runs the other way too: save one life, and it's as if you saved everyone. A paramedic, a lifeguard, a stranger who pulls someone back from the curb. Third, where it's set. The verse begins, for that cause, We decreed for the Children of Israel. It's placed right after the story of Adam's two sons, and given as a decree to an earlier people. It reaches back before Islam, to the family of Adam. The hadith then draw lines even inside war. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Umar reports that a woman was found killed after one of the Prophet's battles, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, forbade the killing of women and children. And in the Muwatta of Imam Malik, Abu Bakr sends an army out with orders: do not kill women, or children, or the old; do not cut down fruit trees. Even in war, there were lines. And outside it, the verse counts one unjust killing as all mankind.
screen: `NAFS: A HUMAN BEING, ANY HUMAN BEING.` · `ONE LIFE COUNTS AS ALL.` · `SET AFTER ADAM'S TWO SONS.` · `EVEN IN WAR, LINES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the victims of violence for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where people have been killed: in the news, in history, in your own city. Don't picture the violence. Picture one person who was there, someone's sister, someone's son, as they were on an ordinary morning. Hold them as a whole world, the way the verse counts them. If you pray, you can pray for them and for those who grieve them, in your own words or in the words you usually use. If you don't, simply keep them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Killing innocents. In Surah al-Ma'idah, to kill one human being unjustly is as if killing all mankind; to save one is as if saving all. Today's word.

Your line: every soul sacred. Today, notice when a news story turns people into a number, and stop to remember one of them as a whole world. Tomorrow, interfaith friendship. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars and preachers cite 5:32 when condemning attacks on civilians, and some mosques hold prayers for victims of violence, whoever they are.

options: even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won't raise mine to kill you.

original.note: Arabic: a soul, a living person; the word Pickthall renders 'a human being' in 5:32.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse about not killing fellow believers.
what it means: killing any human being unjustly is as if killing all mankind, and saving one is as if saving all.
what a scholar hears: nafs in 5:32, set after Adam's sons in 5:27–31 and framed as a decree to the Children of Israel; then the hadith in al-Bukhari and Abu Bakr's orders in the Muwatta on war.
